item.title: How IT Companies Can Survive When Everyone Has AI
item.description:
Not long ago, the question was 'how do we implement neural networks.' Now it's 'how do we survive when everyone has neural networks.' These are different questions. When a powerful tool is available to everyone, it ceases to be an advantage and becomes the entry price to the market. Below are six considerations about what will remain valuable in IT when wrappers around third-party models are no longer an advantage. Read more

item.title: Trusting an AI Agent with Your Server and Sleeping Soundly Without SSH
item.description:
We are moving faster towards self-healing infrastructure. But when an incident does happen, it can take engineers a lot of time to gather information about server status. With 99.99% SLA, there are about 4 minutes left per month for downtime, every minute counts, and not automating this part of incident analysis is an unaffordable luxury. Technically, this can be done now: give the AI agent SSH and sudo. I decided to go a different way and built the Linux MCP daemon (mcpd): a server initially designed for AI agents. Instead of wrappers around standard utilities, it reads system status directly from the kernel and provides it to the agent through tools - there are currently 38 of them, and the list is growing. When root is needed, the agent can request it, but will only get it where you allow it, and within specified boundaries. The linuxctl utility in the style of kubectl turned out to be a separate interesting solution. Under the cut is the architecture, installation, connecting an AI agent, and permissions that only look safe. Read on.

item.title: And what do LLMs themselves think about having consciousness?
item.description:
Discussions about LLMs in mass culture can currently be divided into two broad categories - techno-optimists and techno-alarmists. Techno-optimists are primarily interested in how AI can simplify their lives here and now - at work or in everyday life. Techno-alarmists are primarily interested in the consequences of AI proliferation for society. Job losses, increased political and economic instability, and even existential risks. But it seems to me that both are missing the elephant in the room. We have a certain entity (LLM) that can solve almost the entire spectrum of intellectual tasks that historically only beings with quite advanced thinking and consciousness could solve - that's us, humans. And this prospect seems mind-blowing, as if we encountered alien intelligence, but created it ourselves on a computer through programming. Sci-fi, but not in bad literature, but in real life. I had an idea to ask the language models themselves if they feel anything at all, and even create a humorous benchmark for it with a list of questions, and run different models through it. It is clear that LLMs will most likely duplicate either the position of the developers who trained them, or simply the average position from the internet, but who knows, maybe something interesting will come of it? I AM ALIVE ?

item.title: From University to Artificial Intelligence: How the Invention Generator Accelerated
item.description:
Not the history of all human inventions, but a single conditional trajectory: how the Western scientific and technical system repeatedly expanded the space of subsequent possible solutions. If we look at human history on a cosmic scale, the difference between a person who simply wanted to stay warm by the fire and an engineer at a nuclear power plant seems almost like the blink of an eye. If we exaggerate this image to a joke, it becomes extremely rapid: a hypothetical Cro-Magnon is still thinking about how to get warm, and in a historical instant, his descendants already have a nuclear power plant running. Of course, tens of thousands of years, a huge number of cultures, wars, migrations, discoveries, and vanished branches lie between these points. But the contrast itself is useful: biologically, humans have not turned into a different species during this time, while the external machine for knowledge production has grown enormously. It is this external machine that interests me in this article. I am not trying to retell the history of human inventions, nor am I proposing a universal periodization of civilizations. There will be no separate study of Ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, India, or other great scientific traditions, although their contribution is enormous and many of their achievements have entered the European lineage. For our task, it is sufficient to consciously narrow the field and look at one realized trajectory – the one that, from the late Middle Ages onwards, gradually formed the modern Western and North Atlantic scientific and technical world. Such a limitation is not a statement about the superiority of this trajectory, nor an attempt to declare it the only viable one. It is a research perspective. In the book "The Firm's Brain: 2026," viability is considered not as a single predetermined route, but as a field of continuations: it is important not only what option exists now, but also what possibilities it leaves behind, how independent they are, and how much it costs to keep them open. I am transferring this idea to history solely as a way of posing the question: which institutions, technologies, and ways of organizing knowledge not only yielded immediate results but also expanded the field of subsequent results? Read more

item.title: How do you even live without POWERLINK...
item.description:
B&R process automation after sanctions, without magic and rituals: how to replace a dead controller with a mini-PC, keep the original racks, and not rewrite the project. Driver for Intel I226 network cards, real-time gateway, kernel for the task, and testing on real hardware. In the first article, I talked about how I was left alone with two hundred car washes. It was about why it all worked out. Here it will be about how exactly, with the specifics that were asked for in the comments. First, some context to understand where everything came from. Our car wash automation project is written in Automation Studio, which is B&R's development environment, and it runs on a B&R controller. When it became clear that controllers and modules could no longer be bought, we started migrating projects to regular PCs. For new car washes, this has been debugged since 2022: about a hundred facilities run on mini-PCs, and instead of B&R racks, they have racks from another manufacturer, using Modbus TCP. The project remains the same, only reconfigured for new modules. But this won't work for the old car washes. They have original B&R racks, and they communicate with the controller via POWERLINK. This is a hard real-time protocol with a cycle of two milliseconds, and it wasn't there for show: the PLC counted the flow meter pulses and generated dispenser pulses on it. On such facilities, it's usually the controller that dies, while the racks live on and are ready to serve for another ten years. It's a shame and expensive to replace them, buying a controller is also expensive; a used one through gray import costs from half a million to three and a half million rubles, and that's for each failure. This article is about this case: how to put a mini-PC instead of a controller and not touch the racks or the project itself. Read more

item.title: Browser translator that teaches words: Chrome's built-in Translator API, your own AI key, and spaced repetition
item.description:
There was a popular Chinese extension Dadda Translate (达达划词翻译): you highlight a word, get a translation, save it to a vocabulary list, and the word later pops up as a notification until you memorize it. It stopped working: the Sogou and Shanbay APIs, which powered the translation, changed or disappeared. Moreover, it was only for Chrome and only for English → Chinese. I rewrote it from scratch. The result is WordToast for Firefox, Chrome, and Edge (GitHub). It translates to the browser's language, can work entirely on-device, and explains words in context using your own AI key. In the article, I will discuss three technical parts: How it works

item.title: Why Make a Model Suffer?
item.description:
Researchers gave a language model two buttons. One did nothing. The second was supposed to relieve the model of an unpleasant internal state—sometimes at the cost of worsening the next response or even harming the user. The model chose relief. And if the button didn't work, it tried again. This is not a thought experiment. In the preprint The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It, researchers tried to find a state within language models that functions similarly to pain. The work does not prove that LLMs are conscious or truly suffer. Moreover, the authors explicitly warn of alternative explanations for the results. But the study is interesting for another reason: instead of another conversation with the model about its "feelings," scientists began to study internal activations and causally influence them. Perhaps this is where the answer to the question of AI consciousness lies. Read more

item.title: Generation of the Rejected: How AI Resume Screening Pushes Youth Towards Cybercrime
item.description:
I got my diploma, sent out my first 50 applications, and ran into the classic paradox: to get a job, you need experience, and to get experience, you need a job. I decided to look at the bigger picture: how difficult is it for young specialists to enter IT, what role do automated screening and neural networks play, and can the lack of a clear legal career path become a risk factor for turning to cybercrime? The article includes statistics from the Russian labor market, data on computer crime, research from Criminal Hackers, and my perspective on how hiring needs to change in the age of AI. Read more

item.title: A Mobile Phone from Almost Nothing: How AI Helped Assemble a Phone from Marketplace Parts
item.description:
Today we're building our own mobile phone from readily available materials bought on various marketplaces, with the help of artificial intelligence. We'll clarify upfront that this isn't about creating another iPhone killer or ultra-budget internet access. A simple calling phone is cheaper and easier to buy at the nearest mobile carrier store. Although I can write code to some extent myself, we'll be actively using AI here. Primarily, to save time and avoid delving into the protocols for communicating with the radio module – information that will likely never be needed again. I'll note that I only used the free versions of DeepSeek, Gemini, and ChatGPT in their limited free modes. There was no specific system for when or to whom to ask questions. I usually switched between them when one started to lag. So, to connect to a mobile network, you primarily need a radio module. I don't think I need to explain that soldering one from discrete components is an endeavor with no chance of successful implementation within a reasonable timeframe and budget. It's easier to buy a ready-made radio module. I chose this one: Read more

item.title: Small Language Models: Where SLMs are Useful and What to Consider When Working with Them
item.description:
Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly in the spotlight: at first glance, they are almost as good as LLMs, while using significantly fewer resources. But, as always, there's a catch (and not just one): we discuss whether SLMs are really that good, where they can be truly useful, and where they still struggle. We also explore why, in our opinion, they are unlikely to become serious competitors to LLMs anytime soon. Read more

item.title: Docker for the Paranoid: Organizing SSH Access for a Rootless Container Without Transferring the Private Key
item.description:
SSH access is used in many scenarios, from working with repositories to automation and server management. But if the private key is available to the application itself, it can be stolen if the process is compromised. Replacing SSH with a token doesn't solve the problem: it will just be another secret accessible to the same process. In this article, we'll explore an architecture based on ssh-agent and rootless Docker, where a process can fully utilize granted SSH access without obtaining the private key itself. This restriction is enforced by the access scheme itself and remains even if the software inside the container is compromised. This approach is particularly relevant for systems with AI agents and additional API layers like MCP servers. Read more
